extraction_notes: Source: Randolph Union Course Catalog SY 2026-2027 (Version 1.0), a browser print of a Google Doc; the PDF text has stray zero-width characters, split drop-cap letters (repaired in course names and at the start of descriptions) and, in many justified paragraphs, words run together without spaces (e.g. 'TheDigitalFilmmaking/MediaArts...'); descriptions were copied as extracted, spacing only repaired where the drop-cap was split. Course lengths come from the 'Full Year Course' / 'Semester Course' lines; the catalog states no per-course credits so credits are null. Grades are given only where stated (course name, 'Junior/Senior English Courses', 'open to students in grades...', typical sequence prose). Included beyond regular courses: PBL and CBL offerings, Student Supports classes (Literacy and Math Extensions, Structured Study), Multiple Pathways programs (Early College, Dual Enrollment, Dartmouth CHSP, Work-Based Learning, VTVLC, ILOs), Senior Project, and Randolph Technical Career Center programs (level CTE, name and description given; RTCC refers readers to orangesouthwest.org/rtcc for current descriptions). Courses under 'Future Offerings' (AP Biology, Physics, French III, French culture PBL, Music Exploration, Electronic Music & Sound Production) are included with an offering_note and may not run in 2026-27. Skipped as middle-school-only: Middle School Art (grades 7-8) and the RU Middle School Program of Study overview; High School Chorus/Middle School Chorus is one record. Music for The People PBL appears in both the PBL section and Fine Arts > Music: one record. The CBL intro text names 'Manufacturing & Design I' and 'Manufacturing, Design, & Entrepreneurship II' and a Science note names 'Entrepreneurship & Manufacturing', which differ from the listed Manufacturing 1/2; only listed courses were extracted. The separate undated Proficiency-Based Graduation handbook (catalogs/randolph-union-high-school/grad_requirements_undated.pdf, mentions a 2022 graduate) was used only to cross-check graduation requirements; it states 3 years Social Studies, 2 years World Language, 1.5 years Fine Arts and 'additional elective credits', which differ from the 2026-27 catalog table, so the catalog's figures are used and the differences recorded in graduation_requirements.other. No total credit count is stated in either document. Two remaining check warnings (Structured Study Classes, Culinary Arts: 15-17% of phrases not in source) are false positives: both descriptions are verbatim, but the source text has the first letter of the entry (S) or of a word split across a page break (m|enu) as a separate drop-cap line, which breaks the phrase matching around those words.

courses.description: Literacy and math extensions are smaller group opportunities built into student schedules where students receive additional instruction focused on specific skills. Placement in extensions is based on teacher, family, and student feedback/requests, testing data, and grades. Some students may access this support for a quarter or a semester, while others may access this support throughout the year.

Structured study classes are taught by classroom teachers, and are focused on providing executive functioning and time management support. In addition to practicing specific executive functioning strategies, students will also have time to work on assignments, read, and practice other academic and life skills.

courses.course_name: Early College at Vermont State Colleges, CCV, and Norwich University
courses.description: With the 2013 passage of the Flexible Pathways bill ( Act 77 ), Vermont's Early College Program has expanded with funds being made available to students for programs that are operated or overseen by one of the Vermont State Colleges or by an accredited private post secondary school located in Vermont. Juniors are introduced to the Norwich, VTSU, and CCV Early College Programs through advisory. To begin this process, students need to speak with their school counselor, schedule a meeting with their parents and complete the Early College Advisement Form.
courses.provider: Vermont State Colleges, CCV, Norwich University

courses.course_name: Dual Enrollment at Vermont State Colleges and CCV
courses.description: High school juniors and seniors are eligible to take two college courses at Vermont colleges and universities tuition-free. Please see your school counselor for more information. Students most often take classes through CCV, as their online catalog is extensive, therefore, classes do not interfere with their RU schedule. This allows students to access a college class at times that work best for their schedule.

courses.course_name: Community High School Program (CHSP) at Dartmouth College
courses.description: The Community High School Program at Dartmouth College allows eligible seniors to take one course per term during the fall, winter and spring terms. Juniors may enroll during winter and spring terms only. Students must be recommended by a high school principal, counselor or school official. The tuition for this program is free to the student. Students are responsible for their books and transportation.
courses.notes: program; seniors may take one course per term in fall, winter and spring; juniors winter and spring only

courses.description: Work-based learning at RU is possible through our Independent Learning Opportunity (ILO) program. The school maintains excellent relationships with regional employers. For more information, please see your school counselor.
courses.notes: program; catalog heading 'WBL: Work-Based Learning'; delivered through the Independent Learning Opportunity (ILO) program

courses.description: In an effort to offer expanded course offerings to students, RUHS utilizes the online educational organization called the Vermont Virtual Learning Consortium (VTVLC). VTVLC courses are available to a limited number of students each semester with preference given to seniors and juniors. Sophomores will be considered on a space-available basis. Learn more about VTVLC by visiting vtvlc.org . Interested students should talk with their school counselor about this opportunity.
courses.notes: program; preference given to seniors and juniors, sophomores on a space-available basis

courses.description: RU offers Independent Learning Opportunities to students who wish to explore topics or disciplines in a depth that may be hard to achieve in standard classes. Past ILOs have focused on business management, nonfiction narrative writing, architectural drawing, sports journalism, goat farming, veterinary science, genetic modification, engineering and watershed studies using the Innovation Space, sports nutrition, pre-season training, and a variety of foreign languages and cultures. Strong Habits of Work are a must – an independent work ethic is vital to student success in an ILO - and a “teacher of record” must approve the plan of study in accordance with the student handbook. An ILO is individually titled and can really make a student transcript or resume stand out. See a school counselor or our Director of Career Development and Flexible Pathways for more information.

Senior Project consists of six parts, all of which must be completed in a satisfactory manner and in strict compliance with the deadlines on the Senior Project Timeline. In May, a review panel will evaluate the entire year’s work. The six parts of the Senior Project are as follows: 1. PROPOSAL In the spring of junior year, each student presents a proposal to a panel for mandated pre-approval in an area of study that challenges him or her and holds his or her interest during the yearlong process. The proposal includes a letter of intent, a working bibliography, a research question web, a signed mentor agreement and a parent permission form. The senior presents a proposal to a panel of community members and staff. The senior and his or her panel reach an agreement about what the Senior Project will be. (See Sr. Project Manual for more information.) 2. PAPER Each senior writes a 7 to 12 page research paper on a topic related to the Senior Project. 3. PRODUCT Each senior creates a learning experience that requires spending at least thirty (30) hours using knowledge gained from research and from working with a mentor. 4. PORTFOLIO The portfolio documents the process and journey the student used to complete his or her Senior Project. It will include the following: . documents pertaining to Senior Project a b. time sheet that records the time spent working on the product and a summary of what was accomplished during that time c. journal reflecting on the work, the process and personal growth 5. DISPLAY The Celebration of Learning in May will include the entire portfolio and product. The product might not be tangible; for example, the student might spend time tutoring or working at a service agency, but the portfolio will document what was done. Documentation might include photographs, videotape, or a slide show. Some students wish to participate in a performance as part of the documentation of their product. This usually takes place during the Night of the Arts in May. The Senior Project Open House in May is open for viewing by parents, students, panel members and the public. 6. DEFENSE Each senior will present an eight to ten minute oral defense of his or her entire Senior Project to the panel in May. The oral defense is followed by a five- to eight-minute question and answer period. I f a senior does not complete any one of the five parts in a satisfactory manner or does not meet one of the published deadlines, the student and his/her parent(s) will be notified that the senior is ineligible to graduate in June. At that point the senior may appeal to continue in the Senior Project process. (See Sr. Project Manual for more information.) Senior Project is an important way for students – and our community – to engage in an exciting learning process that allows our students to demonstrate the independent learning skills they have cultivated over their time at Randolph Union.
courses.fulfills_text: Students must also complete a Senior Project to graduate (see graduation requirements)
courses.notes: program; graduation requirement for all students (RTCC students complete the RTCC Project instead)

courses.description: Why do some people have so much more than they need while others struggle to meet their basic needs? How do poverty and inequality affect individuals and our society as a whole? What would an economically just society look like? And what can we do about it, starting right here in Randolph? These are some of the questions we will be digging into in this PBL challenge, which will engage frequently with community members whose work or life experience touches on these issues. Students in this PBL will work collaboratively to analyze the sources of poverty and inequality in our community, and develop projects aimed at addressing these problems. At times, the class may collaborate with other PBLs engaging in similar work, including the Racial Justice PBL and the Food Systems PBL, and with RTCC Culinary through EJ’s Randolph Refuel program. This class might appeal to students interested in economics, personal finance, politics, social sciences, community service, and/or social justice work. This class carries elective credit but, on a case-by-case basis, students may apply to take this class for Social Studies credit. Career Pathways : This PBL challenge will appeal to students interested in career fields such as economics,social sciences,advocacy,human services, political science,community organizing.
courses.fulfills_text: This class carries elective credit but, on a case-by-case basis, students may apply to take this class for Social Studies credit.
courses.notes: PBL; Social Studies standards; challenge question: How can we work toward a more economically just society?

courses.description: In this PBL challenge, students will develop their musicianship while exploring the diversity of music for the small ensemble through writing and arranging music. In addition, students will delve into music and culture, both in historical and contemporary timelines, to better understand the role of music in creating community, change-making, and storytelling. The PBL will conclude with a student-designed performance that extends beyond the classroom and provides for connection to the wider-community. Career Pathways : This PBL challenge will appeal to students interested in career fields such as music, arts, theater, sound production, education.
courses.notes: PBL; Performing arts standards; challenge question: How does music fit into our daily life and the life of your community?; also listed under Fine Arts > Music

courses.course_name: RU Youth Policy Lab- Rock the Vote
courses.description: With declining population throughout the state, how can we create a community that truly embraces youth voice and provides for creating a community that young people will want to return to after post-secondary studies and training? In this PBL challenge, students will focus on expanding youth participation in local government. In exploring how democratic systems work at the local level, including how policies are created, how voting laws are established, and how citizens advocate for change within their communities. Students will research youth voting policies in other towns and countries, analyze arguments for and against lowering the voting age, and examine the role of civic participation in a healthy democracy. Using these skills, the class will collaborate on a real-world civic action project: developing and implementing a campaign to advocate for lowering the voting age to 16 in Randolph. By the end of the challenge, students will have gained hands-on experience in civic engagement and a deeper understanding of how individuals can influence public policy in their communities. Career Pathways : This PBL challenge will appeal to students interested in career fields such as economics,social sciences,law, advocacy,human services, political science,community organizing.
courses.notes: PBL; Social Studies/English standards; challenge question: How can students gain a deserved seat at the table in shaping their community?

courses.description: In this media focused PBL challenge, students will be leading the charge in researching, creating, editing, and publishing bi-weekly media content for the school and surrounding community in conjunction with local media outlets. Deliverables will include both traditional forms of news publications (lead stories, opinion pieces, social commentary, sports and community event coverage) and contemporary digital content (podcasts, video reporting, social media). The focus of this PBL will be geared towards establishing and sustaining a forum for students to share their experiences and perspectives with the wider community in an authentic, self-directed manner featuring a diversity of viewpoints. In the pursuit of this goal, students will explore the roles and responsibilities of media in informing the public about important local and societal issues while collaborating and learning from professionals. Career Pathways: This PBL will appeal to students who are interested in media, political science, social commentary, community engagement, history, and communications.
courses.notes: PBL; Social Studies/English standards; challenge question: How can students create and maintain a dialogue with their broader community through media publications?

courses.course_name: RU RJ: Many Voices, Many Histories
courses.description: In this PBL Challenge, students will respond to increasing concerns about social and racial injustice in our local and national communities. Students will work with area experts to raise awareness around racial and social injustice to create a safer and more educated environment for all community members. In addition to establishing and maintaining a racial & social justice student alliance here at RU, students will reflect on the history of social injustice in our country. Through the PBL, students will work with their peers to educate our school and wider community about current issues. Throughout the year, students will work to develop a robust student group, establish goals, participate in field work, and host events and workshops. In participating in this PBL, students will learn about organizing around social issues and advocating for change through education and action. This class carries elective credit but, on a case-by-case basis, students may apply to take this class for English or Social Studies credit based on teacher of record availability. Career Pathways : This PBL challenge will appeal to students interested in careers in social justice, community organizing, social work, political science, history, and education.
courses.fulfills_text: This class carries elective credit but, on a case-by-case basis, students may apply to take this class for English or Social Studies credit based on teacher of record availability.
courses.notes: PBL; Elective standards; challenge question: How can we advocate for and create a more equitable community?

courses.description: Have you ever wondered how the products you buy make it to the store shelves? Whether it’s video games, clothing, or sports equipment, the goods we purchase must go through a manufacturing process. In this course, you’ll learn about the types of manufacturing systems and processes used to create the products we buy every day.

This will be a continuation of the curriculum from Manufacturing 1. Students will apply the practices from Manufacturing 1. They will have a chance to work on their skills with different manufacturing projects. Students will also explore different careers in the manufacturing field.

This exploration class looks at the different technologies and processes used in a maker space. Students will design and produce their own projects. This is a good opportunity for students who are self-motivated, independent, and curious about the innovation space.

3D printing is the process of additive manufacturing turning a 3D model (STL) into a physical print. The Innovation Center 3D printers use an additive fabrication process to generate products. Students will be exposed to the process of 3D printing from STL.File to Print. This class will look at how filament is made and spooled before being used on a 3D printer.

The Digital Photography course exposes students to a range of creative digital and media arts projects. This course is a hands-on class where students will learn by collaborating in and outside the classroom. Over the semester students will work on a selection of projects related to: natural world (plants, animals, or the outdoors), cityscapes and structures (man-made structures), people (fashion photography to personal portraits), lifestyle (candid) photography (large occasions to little moments of everyday life), commercial photography skills (food and product photography), artistic shots ( ways to craft intriguing images through different photographic art i.e Black & White/Surreal Photography),and stop motion ( animation).

The goal of this course is for students to increase their ability to read higher level texts. This will be accomplished by students reading a class novel, reading a novel of their choice and a focus on non-fiction text.. This will include discussions and connections to students' lives. Students will also be reading a novel of their choice and writing reflections based on their reading. Furthermore, students will be writing each day focusing on skills that will strengthen their critical thinking in the reading context.
courses.notes: High School and Middle School Sections; English Intervention Elective

courses.description: This course will teach the fundamentals of writing through the lens of children’s books and fairy tales. Students will start by writing simple sentences that use decodable vocabulary to create stories for very young readers, then progress up to more complex sentence structures and narratives that families can enjoy together. Students will write and illustrate their own fictional and informative picture books that they can share with the elementary schools in our district. The class is designed for students who are interested in Early Childhood Education, nostalgic for the days they spent reading picture books, or considering a career in writing, as well as those who would benefit from writing intervention services.

In this class, students will develop their reading, writing, speaking and listening skills by exploring short stories, novels, nonfiction, and poetry. They will investigate how social issues like oppression and poverty affect individuals and communities, and how people come together to find joy and hope despite these challenges. Students will write analytical and persuasive essays as well as creative and personal narratives; discuss. Skills building will focus on active reading strategies and productive writing processes. A range of texts will be used, including short stories, poetry, fiction and nonfiction.

In this class, students will develop their reading, writing, speaking and listening skills by exploring short stories, novels, nonfiction, and poetry. They will investigate how social issues like oppression, poverty, and hierarchies affect individuals and communities, and how people come together to find joy and hope despite these challenges. Students will write analytical and persuasive essays as well as creative and personal narratives; discuss. Skills building will focus on active reading strategies and productive writing processes. A range of texts will be used, including short stories, poetry, fiction and nonfiction.

Advanced Placement Language and Composition is a year-long, college-level English Language Arts course designed to prepare highly motivated students for success on the AP Language exam. It is intended to teach students how to read, analyze, and write about the rhetorical strategies embedded within a broad and challenging range of non-fiction texts. Through frequent informal and formal performance tasks, students will develop the skills necessary to intelligently synthesize arguments from multiple texts into persuasive essays in which they establish strong claims, support them with convincing evidence, thoughtfully explain how their evidence supports their claims, and acknowledge and respond to the most compelling arguments refuting their logic and reasoning. To give shape to the course’s content, readings are organized around themes addressing key cultural, social, and political issues that shape and define our culture today. This class will prepare students for the demanding reading and writing they will encounter in college. Most importantly, though, students will engage in deep critical inquiries into aspects of our world that will help them realize their full potential as active participants in our democratic society. Upon successful performance on the Advanced Placement exam, students may earn up to three college credits and advanced placement in college English. A summer reading and writing assignment is required for enrollment in this course.
courses.notes: Junior/Senior English Courses; Full Year Course (with summer work); summer reading and writing assignment required for enrollment

courses.description: Advanced Placement Literature and Composition is a year-long, college-level English Language Arts course designed to prepare highly motivated students for success on the AP Literature exam. Students will read, analyze, talk, and write about imaginative literature from the Greek and Roman classics to the present to deepen their understanding of how writers use language to cultivate meaning and explore the human condition in their art. They will read texts as authorial constructions—intentional acts of other humans trying to communicate something important to them. Students will understand how crucial it is to respect writers by reading their texts as they expect them to before deciding to what extent they want to embrace, adapt, or resist the writer’s visions. To that end, the key question students will ask throughout the year is: How do writers reveal their thoughts, beliefs, and feelings through their writing? In other words, how do they use writing conventions and literary elements and devices to communicate their ideas? What kinds of changes are writers working to produce in their readers and the world—and why? What points of view or perspectives are writers representing—and why? What are writers encouraging readers to know, believe, or do after reading their texts—and why? This is an engaging and rigorous reading, writing, and discussion-based course of study that requires on-time completion of all formative and summative assessments. Upon successful performance on the Advanced Placement exam, students may earn up to three college credits and advanced placement in college English. A summer reading and writing assignment is required for enrollment in this course.
courses.notes: Junior/Senior English Courses; Full Year Course (with summer work); summer reading and writing assignment required for enrollment

courses.description: The American Dream is a slippery concept. Some argue that every American can experience economic prosperity, social mobility, and personal freedom and happiness if they are willing to apply themselves. Others argue that systematic barriers—such as racism, sexism, the exploitation of the lower and middle classes, and class rigidity—prevent many Americans from achieving it despite their considerable efforts. In this one-semester English Language Arts course, students will analyze the ways in which American authors have questioned their society’s most deeply rooted assumptions and values. While doing so, they will explore and develop intelligent, well-defended responses to the following questions (among others): To what degree is the American Dream real, an expression of nostalgia for a disappearing past, or an idealized narrative of the American experience as a promised land filled with limitless resources and boundless opportunities? To what degree is the American Dream (and its notion of upward mobility) available to everyone in our society or only to those from specific socio-economic backgrounds, races, and sexes, etc.? To what degree has the American Dream evolved? To what degree does American literature shape, respond to, and challenge vital social, political, and cultural conversations? To what degree does American literature compel its readers to become well-informed, active participants in our democracy? With these inquiries in mind, students will read, write, and argue through a variety of performance tasks (e.g., close-reads, class discussions, Socratic seminars, essays, and quick-writes, etc.) grounded in complex texts that may include The Great Gatsby , Of Mice and Men , Death of a Salesman , A Raisin in the Sun , or Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas . Non-fiction texts will augment the study of those mentioned above.

courses.course_name: Narrator Reliability in Literature, Media, and Film
courses.description: In this semester-long English Language Arts course, you’ll examine narrative perspectives to better understand how they shape our notions of truth and reality. Through the lenses of literature, media, and film, you’ll explore how unreliable narrators intentionally and unintentionally manipulate content to influence their audiences’ perceptions—i.e., to persuade them to think or behave in specific ways. The essential questions that will guide instruction are: To what degree can we trust someone else’s (or our own) perception of reality, and how can we discover whether the stories we are told are true? By consistently applying these questions to course materials, you’ll develop a heightened and nuanced awareness of the power dynamics inherent in storytelling. You’ll also cultivate the critical thinking skills necessary to interrogate a variety of narrative texts for implied bias, thereby empowering you to navigate our increasingly complex world with insight and discernment.

We’re all storytellers—even if we haven’t published our writing in a magazine or online journal. We’ve heard and told stories since we were babies and learned about life through them. Understood by the young and old, Once upon a time … and then … and then … and then …and the end are common phrases for signaling a story. Here’s a complication, though: telling a story is one thing—writing one is another. It takes a high level of awareness to understand how stories are formed and how they shape people's perceptions of the world, their sense of self, and their relationships with others.

Dystopian fiction often imagines bleak, apocalyptic futures controlled by totalitarian regimes, subjugated by technology run amok, devastated by environmental disasters, and blighted by plague-like contagions. As depressing as these imagined worlds may seem, they do productive work. By focusing on and exaggerating contemporary social problems, dystopian literature can affect healthy cultural change. In this one-semester English Language Arts course, students will analyze the ways in which dystopian authors turn inquisitive eyes on their societies to improve them. While doing so, they will explore and develop intelligent answers to the following questions (among others): What are the defining characteristics of dystopian fiction? In other words, what themes, symbols, and images recur in the genre? How does dystopian literature respond to, challenge, and shape vital social, political, and cultural conversations? How do governing authorities use propaganda to control the masses, and what responsibility does the individual have to question them? To what degree does dystopian fiction compel readers to become well-informed and active social critics—to realize their potential to change the worlds in which they live? Students will read, write, and argue through various performance tasks requiring them to comprehend, analyze, and evaluate complex, provocative fiction and non-fiction texts that are intended to serve their intellectual, social, and emotional needs.

courses.course_name: The Hero's Journey in Literature and Film
courses.description: The hero’s journey paradigm is a storytelling structure that, at various levels, informs much of the fiction we read and watch. In this one-semester English Language Arts course, students will apply Joseph Campbell’s version of it to a wide range of narratives. This interpretive work is designed to lead students to a deeper understanding of the texts they experience (e.g., the hero’s journey symbols and patterns often embedded in literature, film, music, television, and advertising, etc.), the world in which they live (e.g., its values and ideals), and, ultimately, themselves (e.g., their psychological and emotional struggles and transformations). More than anything, students will cultivate an appreciation for storytelling as a reflection of humankind’s innate longing to create structure, and thus meaning, out of the complex materials of human experience.

In this class, students will explore the history of the United States from the pre-colonial era through the Civil War. Students will learn basic geographical and historical facts about our nation while also exploring broader questions of American identity and rights through a comparison of historical and contemporary events. The course will approach this content from the perspective of multiple socioeconomic classes, races, ethnicities, and genders. This class will also focus on the development of oral proficiencies through classroom discussions, as well as writing skills needed for success at higher grade levels. The course will culminate in a research project, the completion of which is required to complete the course.

Modern World History is a global history course aimed at tenth-grade students that provides a cohesive approach to learning and understanding the history of the world. In this course, students will explore the transformations that created our modern world, beginning in the long nineteenth century and ending in our present moment. This course will help students learn how to use stories about our connected human past to orient themselves to their present moment and prepare for the future. We’re going to cover a lot of ground (and almost 300 years), but this course is not a typical march-through-time history class that covers one thing after another. Rather, this course uses a set of overarching inquiry problems and narrative frames, situated at a variety of scales, to organize and facilitate teaching and learning. Along with presentation summative assessments, students will also complete three document-based writing assignments and a 3-5 page research paper.

This course explores American history from the Reconstruction period through the present day. Using case studies, role plays, seminar discussions, oral history interviews, and independent research, students will explore the events and historical forces that shaped the world we live in today, and evaluate various perspectives about the lessons we should learn from these events to help us make sense of the problems we face today. This class will focus on developing research and writing skills to prepare students for Senior Project, and on developing the knowledge and skills to be informed, engaged citizens.
courses.notes: catalog's typical course sequence places US History II in 11th grade

courses.description: AP U.S. History is designed to be the equivalent of a two-semester introductory college or university U.S. history course. In AP U.S. History, students investigate significant events, individuals, developments, and processes in nine historical periods from approximately 1491 to the present. Students develop and use the same skills, practices, and methods employed by historians: analyzing primary and secondary sources; making historical comparisons; utilizing reasoning about contextualization, causation, and continuity and change over time; and developing historical arguments. The course also provides seven themes that students explore throughout the course in order to make connections among historical developments in different times and places: American and national identity; migration and settlement; politics and power; work, exchange, and technology; America in the world; geography and the environment; and culture and society.

The AP World History course focuses on developing students' understanding of world history from 1200 CE to the present. Students investigate the content of world history for significant events, individuals, developments, and processes in four historical periods, and develop and use the same thinking skills and methods employed by historians when they study the past. The course also provides five themes that students explore throughout the course in order to make connections among historical developments in different times and places encompassing the five major geographical regions of the globe: Africa, the Americas, Europe, Asia, and Oceania. Students will focus much of their energy on preparation for the National Advanced Placement Examination in May.

World Religions takes a look at various belief systems throughout human history, and focuses on five major world religions being practiced today: Hinduism, Buddhism, Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. Students in this course have the opportunity to read and interpret religious texts, discover unfamiliar cultural practices, and identify the significance of religion in shaping the world in which we live. Summative assessments allow students to choose topics of interest within each major religion for deepdive research and presentation, in order to teach the rest of the class about their findings. This is a great elective for students who wish to learn more about history, the power of myth, and its ability to organize culture around the world.

This course provides an introduction to archaeological theory and methods through the study of the Ancestral Puebloan (Anasazi) peoples of the Four Corners Region. Students will explore the development of their civilization from the Archaic era up through Modern Puebloan societies, including the cliff-dwellers of the Pueblo II era. Students will think critically about pseudoarchaeology, focussing on how interpretations of the past that ignore or misrepresent scientific evidence , often promote sensationalist ideas The class will travel to the Crow Canyon Archaeological Center in Cortez, Colorado in October.

This course presents an introductory overview of the history of Western art from the Renaissance to the present. It covers works in a wide array of media, such as painting, sculpture, architecture, prints, photography, and performance. Emphasizing significant stylistic movements in Europe and the Americas, this class introduces students to visual analysis and other interpretative tools of art historical research. Students will also learn how the art pieces of a particular time and place relate to historical circumstances and values of their respective societies. The skills developed in this course provide important tools for navigating and interpreting media and visual representation in the twenty first century.

courses.course_name: Sociology: Nature and Nurture; Rights and Wrongs
courses.description: Once you have taken Sociology, you will never look at the world the same way again. This is because Sociology is not a body of knowledge, but a way of thinking about how human societies function. We’ll ask (and attempt to answer) questions like: “What attributes do all cultures share?” “Are we born with our morals, or do we learn them?” “What are the unwritten rules of social interaction and what happens when they are broken?” and “Under what conditions will ordinary people behave in extraordinarily evil ways?” If you take this course, expect to read, write and share your ideas in class on a regular basis; I promise it won’t be boring, but this is not an elective you can coast through. The final exam will be a research project in which you investigate a topic that interests you, collect and interpret data, and present your findings.

You may think it’s all graphs and numbers. You may think that Economics is boring. You may think that you could never understand terms like “collateralized debt obligations” or “aggregate demand” and that even if you could, it would never help you in your life. But you’d be wrong. This course is tough, but it is also practical, interesting and extremely relevant. By the end of the semester, you will be able to use economics to predict how gas and food prices might change over time, decide how best to pay for college or a car, evaluate politicians’ plans to fix the economy, invest your time and money most effectively, and decide for yourself how worried you should be about our national debt. Completing homework, studying for quizzes and actively participating are keys to success in this course.

In this course students will examine the full scope of Vermont history. We begin with the natural history of the land and the forces that shaped Vermont’s landscapes, and lead into an examination of Vermont’s indigenous populations. From there we look at the arrival of Europeans, and formation of the United States. We will explore Vermont’s role in the greater developments of the nation and the world, while discovering how our local communities reacted to those events. This course will rely heavily on primary sources, allowing students to discover the images and writings from our local history. This course will appeal to students who are interested in their local history, and will ask students to make their own discoveries and evaluations from primary sources, rather than relying on secondary sources or others’ interpretations.

This first class in our series of three courses uses a rigorous integrated problem solving approach to enhance student learning habits through investigation of related topics and skills, much like those one could find in real life. Students develop mathematical reasoning and computation skills through collaboration, critical thinking, and related skills practice. This instruction is supported through an online digital skills support program called Mathia. The content included in AGS 1 includes analysis and manipulation of functions, systems of equations and inequalities, coordinate graphing, one-variable statistics, constructions, and rigid motion congruence theorems.

This second of three course series continues development of the integrated content. Students further develop mathematical reasoning and computation skills through collaboration, critical thinking, and related skills practice. The content includes algebraic analysis of geometric shapes and relationships, trigonometric relationships and applications, and probability.
courses.prerequisites: AGS 1 or equivalent or teacher permission

courses.description: This third of our series of integrated courses. This course includes the structure of algebraic patterns and quadratics, comparisons of polynomial equations and models, rational and irrational functions with logarithmic expressions and modeling, further applications of trigonometry, and data interpretations and arguments using these previous tools.
courses.prerequisites: AGS 2 or equivalent or teacher permission

courses.description: This course is offered as a prerequisite for those students interested in taking Advanced Placement Calculus and college Calculus. The course finishes the study of functions of two variables: polynomial, exponential, logarithmic, trigonometric and the conic sections. Mathematical reasoning, problem solving, understanding multiple perspectives, and use of graphing calculators will be stressed.
courses.prerequisites: AGS 3 and AGS 2 or teacher permission

courses.description: This elective course is equivalent to a first-semester college statistics course. Students will learn concepts and tools for collecting, analyzing and drawing conclusions from data. Students learn under four broad conceptual themes: 1) Exploring Data: Describing patterns and departures from patterns, 2) Sampling and Experimentation: Planning and conducting a study, 3) Anticipating Patterns: Exploring random phenomena using probability and simulation, and 4) Statistical Inference: Estimating population parameters and testing hypotheses. Due to the rigor of the AP curriculum, a non-AP version of statistics will be concurrently offered. Please see the instructor to determine which course placement is most appropriate for you.
courses.notes: Description says the course is equivalent to a first-semester college statistics course; a non-AP version is offered concurrently with the AP curriculum (AP Statistics is listed among available AP courses)

courses.description: This elective course is equivalent to a first-semester college calculus course. Students will engage in the following behaviors to achieve conceptual understanding: reasoning with definitions and theorems, connecting concepts and representations, implementing processes, building notational fluency, and communication of ideas. As prescribed by the College Board, students will study three main ideas: limits, derivatives, and integrals. The notion of a limit helps us understand the behavior of a graph near a point and serves as the basis for determining continuity. In a hopeful sense, limits are much less about what things are and much more about what things should be. Derivatives give us the language of covariation: describing the rate of change of one variable in terms of another variable. Applications of derivatives include, but are not limited to, slopes of tangent lines at a point, analyzing graphs, rectilinear motion, Mean Value Theorem, related rates, optimization, and growth and decay. Integrals allow students to use the language of limits to solve problems involving area, volume, rectilinear motion, and accumulation. Students will study the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus as means to translate between the languages of derivatives and integrals. Due to the rigor of the AP curriculum, a non-AP version of calculus will be concurrently offered. Please see the instructor to determine which course placement is most appropriate for you.
courses.notes: Elective; a non-AP version of calculus is offered concurrently

courses.description: AP Computer Science Principles is an introductory college-level computing course that introduces students to the breadth of the field of computer science. Students learn to design and evaluate solutions and to apply computer science to solve problems through the development of algorithms and programs. They incorporate abstraction into programs and use data to discover new knowledge. Students also explain how computing innovations and computing systems—including the internet—work, explore their potential impacts, and contribute to a computing culture that is collaborative and ethical. The following are the major areas of study, or big ideas, that serve as the foundation of the course, enabling students to create meaningful connections among concepts and develop deeper conceptual understanding: Creative Development: When developing computing innovations, developers can use a formal, iterative design process or a less rigid process of experimentation, and will encounter phases of investigating and reflecting, designing, prototyping, and testing Data: Data are central to computing innovations because they communicate initial conditions to programs and represent new knowledge. Algorithms and Programming: Programmers integrate algorithms and abstraction to create programs for creative purposes and to solve problems. ■ Computing Systems and Networks: Computer systems and networks are used to transfer data. Impact of Computing: Computers and computing have revolutionized our lives. To use computing safely and responsibly, we need to be aware of privacy, security, and ethical issues. During this full year course students will create many programs using JavaScript which is considered by many experts to be the among the most commonly used computer language in the world today.

This course provides an introduction to robotics for students with no programming background using Vex Robotic kits. Using the CCSS math practices, students will learn to construct, control and program these robots through investigative and exploration activities. Research projects will expose the students to the engineering process.

This course will continue the development of the engineering skills necessary to advance previous robot programs and design. Students use mentoring to increase their understanding of required programs. More rigorous research projects or activities will be expected. Students may partake in the regional Vex Robotics competition.
courses.prerequisites: the successful completion of Robotics I or equivalent experience

courses.description: Students in this class build their numeracy skills, hone problem-solving strategies, and work with resources geared to, and differentiated for, individual needs. Common Core Math Practice Standards are reinforced throughout this course. Along with increased mathematical competency students will practice their organizational skills, note-taking strategies, personal management skills, productivity, reflection and revision. Areas of focus include financial literacy, architecture, and foundational skills.

courses.course_name: Integrated Science I: Earth Science with Chemistry
courses.description: This course serves as an introduction to Earth science with an emphasis on the chemistry of and human impact on the environment. We will examine surface and atmospheric processes including, but not limited to, the relationships between resource extraction, natural hazards, and climate change and human development. We will use hands-on investigations and real world examples to explore these key concepts.

courses.course_name: Integrated Science II: Biology with Chemistry
courses.description: This course offers an introduction to the principles of biology with emphasis on biological chemistry, ecology and homeostasis, cell structure and function, gene expression, and patterns of inheritance. We will be using hands-on labs and real-world examples to explore the key concepts in biology.
courses.prerequisites: Integrated Science I: Earth Science with Chemistry

courses.description: This course considers questions such as “how did the Universe begin? How do stars generate the different elements that make up our world? How did the Earth form, and how does energy from the Sun’s core arrive here?” This course provides an introduction to the principles of physics through the lens of space. We will be using hands-on investigations to analyze the phenomena of space. ( RU students at RTCC also take the semester of Integrated Science III to help ensure coverage of standards and help with their readiness for the 11th grade assessment.)
courses.prerequisites: Integrated Science I: Earth Science with Chemistry Chemistry Full Year Course This course offers a foundation in chemical concepts and focuses on physical chemistry. Students will learn how the atom and its particles determine the nature and properties of compounds that make our world work. This course has a heavy emphasis on science skills including explanations and argumentation, developing and conducting investigations, and reading informational texts. Basic algebra skills will be employed to better understand the content; dimensional analysis is the backbone of most calculations. This course will help students who wish to take AP Physics and AP Biology. Prerequisite: Integrated Science 1 and AGS 1 or instructor approval

courses.description: This course offers a foundation in chemical concepts and focuses on physical chemistry. Students will learn how the atom and its particles determine the nature and properties of compounds that make our world work. This course has a heavy emphasis on science skills including explanations and argumentation, developing and conducting investigations, and reading informational texts. Basic algebra skills will be employed to better understand the content; dimensional analysis is the backbone of most calculations. This course will help students who wish to take AP Physics and AP Biology.
courses.prerequisites: Integrated Science 1 and AGS 1 or instructor approval

courses.description: This course follows the College Board Curriculum for AP Physics 1. It offers both hands-on and theoretical approaches to understanding forces, momentum and energy and applying them to everyday situations. Topics covered include kinematics, projectile motion, statics and dynamics, rotational mechanics, pressure and fluids. Algebra is used throughout this course as mathematics is the backbone of physics. Students who are interested in engineering, technical or science careers are encouraged to take this class.

AP Environmental Science is an interdisciplinary course that focuses on ecological processes, human impacts on the earth, and how to resolve or prevent natural and human-made environmental problems. Students who complete the course will be expected to apply scientific concepts, principles, and methodologies to real-world examples and problems.

Applied Science is a hands-on, project-based course that explores how scientific concepts are used in the real-world. Students investigate a variety of fields including health sciences, environmental science, engineering, diversified agriculture, forensic science, and skilled trades through practical applications and problem-solving experiences. Each unit is organized around a specific career pathway, allowing students to engage in authentic tasks such as designing solutions, conducting experiments, analyzing data, and using industry-relevant tools and techniques. Emphasis is placed on developing transferable skills including critical thinking, collaboration, communication, and scientific/technical literacy.

This semester-long course will introduce students to forensic science, and skills and practices used in crime scene investigation and other applied sciences. Students will learn how to investigate, and problem solve with lab activities and mock crime scenes, as well as explore the many careers paths and applications of this science.

In this semester-long course, you will learn how CORAL REEFS, SEAGRASS BEDS and MANGROVE FORESTS support specialized forms of ocean life and how they support one another as well. Also, learn how we, as humans, can contribute considerably in the preservation of marine organisms/systems that support overall EARTH-HEALTH. This course may culminate in a week-long marine biology field-trip.

This semester-long course will take you on a walk through the human body seeing human tissues magnified 400 times with HIGH-POWERED MICROSCOPES and learn how your many billions of cells work together to allow you to do all the interesting things you do. Everything from seeing, hearing, tasting, smelling and the way your body parts work together to perform exercise will be explored.

The goal of this course is to help students develop a foundation in college-level biology. Students will engage as scientists in systematically investigating the world around us and building on the understanding of prior scientific work. In addition to appreciating the inherent beauty and elegance of living beings, throughout the course students will make connections between ideas in the course as well as to current societal issues. Daily use of scientific thinking will help students explore concepts in an authentic context while honing key skills. Students will be expected to take the exam in May.
courses.prerequisites: Proficiency in science standards 1 - 3 or approval from the instructor.

courses.description: French I is a beginning level language course designed to develop basic speaking, reading, writing and listening skills. Students will focus on building vocabulary and grammar, as well as an awareness of the history, geography, culture, and ways of life in various French-speaking countries of the world. The cultural focus of this class is meant to highlight France and their cultural heritage. Students will be able to ask simple questions, talk about themselves and their environment and will be able to grasp the meaning of simple texts, videos, and songs in French.

This course reviews and expands on the basic communicative skills taught in French I. Students will be capable of more complex conversational exchanges in the present tense. Students will progress from memorized words and phrases to “sentence-level” dialogue to “paragraph-level” conversations and will become comfortable reading and responding to longer texts in French. Students will focus on building vocabulary and grammar, as well as an awareness of the history, geography, culture, and ways of life in various French-speaking countries of the world. Students will use more complex structures to ask questions and express opinions. The course will have a cultural and linguistic focus on music and food.

Spanish I is a beginning level language course designed to develop basic speaking, reading, writing and listening skills. Students will focus on building vocabulary and grammar, as well as an awareness of the history, geography, culture, and ways of life in various Spanish-speaking countries of the world. The cultural focus of this class is meant to introduce students to the world’s many Spanish-speaking countries and their cultural heritage. Students will be able to ask simple questions, talk about themselves and their environment and will be able to grasp the meaning of simple texts, videos, and songs in Spanish.

This course reviews and expands on the basic communication skills and cultural knowledge from Spanish I. Students will be capable of more complex conversational exchanges in the present tense, and will develop their listening comprehension skills and be encouraged to increase their speaking skills. They will progress from “sentence –level” dialog to “paragraph –level” conversations and will become comfortable reading and responding to longer texts in Spanish. The course will have a cultural and linguistic focus on music and food.

Students in this course will review the grammar principles learned in Spanish I and II and consider new themes not presented there. Reading, writing and conversational skills will be sharpened as we study the history, geography and culture of several of the twenty Spanish-speaking countries in the world. Using Spanish in class is a priority at this level and students will be reading and responding to stories, films, podcasts, songs, and other authentic media from the Spanish-speaking world. Students will create dialogues, videos, and presentations in which they talk about the past, present, and future. Students will continue developing their ability to communicate in Spanish, expanding on the grammar and vocabulary from previous years through thematic cultural units that deepen their knowledge of history and culture and address current issues. In addition, students will focus on improving written communication. They will write short essays in response to cultural events and issues in the United States and Spanish-speaking countries. Readings, films, class discussion and music will facilitate their understanding of the language. The class will also incorporate group activities and accessible technology. At the end of the year students will have deepened their understanding of the language and have a broader knowledge of the cultures, art, history and literature of the Spanish-speaking world.

This class is designed to expand upon the material covered in French I and II, as well as begin to use more authentic texts and resources to expose students to a wider variety of topics beyond personal environments and relationships. Reading, writing and conversational skills will be sharpened as we study the history, geography and culture of several of the 29 French-speaking countries in the world. Using French in class is a priority at this level and students will be reading and responding to stories, films, podcasts, and authentic media from the French-speaking world. Students will create dialogues, videos, and presentations in which they talk about the past, present, and future. Through the study of authentic sources, students gain an appreciation for the breadth of cultures, beliefs and customs across the francophone world.

courses.course_name: Oh la, la, la-French Culture, Cuisine and Conversation PBL
courses.description: In this PBL challenge, students will continue to work on their French communication skills while exploring the rich traditions of French culinary arts. In exploring social customs and norms of food culture, both historical and contemporary in France.Then we will look into how those were brought to countries colonized by the French and how the food traditions of those colonies influenced French food culture.Additionally, students will extend language learning through service and collaborative work, while building community. Career Pathways: This PBL challenge will appeal to students interested in career fields such as political science, anthropology, social sciences, foreign language, French literature, and culinary arts.

courses.department: Fine Arts: Visual Arts, Music, Theater
courses.description: Strict deadlines need to be met in order to produce professional quality publications, so this course will require good attendance, athletic/event attendance, and multi-tasking skills. Assignments will be within the school and students are expected to attend and photograph at least 3 athletic home games. Students will learn basic skills to create our printed yearbook. This includes the basics of photography, camera usage, and compositional skills. We will also focus on layout, color theory, typography and page design. Assignments will include interviewing techniques, caption writing, and printed story methods; including polls, surveys, feature stories, and headline construction. Good social skills are needed as you will be running errands around the school and conducting interviews with fellow staff and students. A special emphasis will be on staying organized, teamwork, critiquing, editing, and meeting authentic deadlines.

courses.department: Fine Arts: Visual Arts, Music, Theater
courses.description: Elements of Art is a foundational high school visual arts course designed to introduce students to the core principles and building blocks of artistic expression. Students will explore the seven elements of art—line, shape, form, space, color, value, and texture—through hands-on projects using a variety of traditional media. Emphasis is placed on creativity, experimentation, skill development, and visual literacy.

courses.department: Fine Arts: Visual Arts, Music, Theater
courses.description: Principles of Art builds on foundational skills with a focused exploration of the principles of design: balance, contrast, emphasis, movement, pattern, rhythm, and unity. While students do not need to be “advanced” artists, the course challenges them to think more critically about composition and visual organization. Through a variety of media and project-based work, students will learn how to intentionally apply design principles to create more dynamic and meaningful artwork.

courses.department: Fine Arts: Visual Arts, Music, Theater
courses.description: Band is for students who enjoy making music with friends! By playing instruments in various styles and settings, students will improve their ability to perform on their instrument, both alone and with others. All instruments are welcome! Band members will participate in various concerts throughout the year at which participation is required. Students will also have the opportunity to audition for both the Winooski Valley District Music Festival and the All-State Music Festival. Instrumental proficiency and music experience is a prerequisite for this class.

courses.department: Fine Arts: Visual Arts, Music, Theater
courses.description: This class is a great opportunity for students to learn a new instrument or get better at the one that they have been playing. Band members will learn the fundamentals of playing their instruments, reading music, and how to play with others in an ensemble. Advanced players will be able to participate in the Winooski Valley Music Festivals. All skill levels are welcome!
courses.notes: Music; catalog grade range 7-9, only grade 9 is high school

courses.course_name: High School Chorus Grades 9-12 / Middle School Chorus Grades 7 & 8
courses.department: Fine Arts: Visual Arts, Music, Theater
courses.description: Chorus is open to all students who like to sing! Proper methods of vocal production, listening, expression and musicianship are emphasized. Music from differing periods, composers, styles and cultures will be covered, exposing students to different languages, forms and eras of music. Participants learn to read music notation. Chorus members will participate in various concerts throughout the year at which participation is required. Students will also have the opportunity to audition for both the Winooski Valley District Music Festival and the All-State Music Festival. Prior experience is not a requirement.

courses.department: Fine Arts: Visual Arts, Music, Theater
courses.description: Music theory & composition combines in-depth learning of melody, harmony, rhythm, form, analysis and composition for those who wish to gain a deeper understanding of how music works. Students will practice these skills through reading, writing, listening to, and analyzing classical and contemporary popular music. Students will develop ear training skills with regular sight reading and sight singing practice and will apply all theory concepts learned in the form of compositions using FlatIo music notation software. This is a course for the serious music student.

courses.department: Fine Arts: Visual Arts, Music, Theater
courses.description: This course is designed to introduce students to the fundamentals of music through hands-on exploration of a variety of units to include: musical instruments (percussion, keyboard, and guitar) music theory, music production, film and video game music analysis, and popular music. Students will develop basic music reading and listening skills, ensemble awareness, and an appreciation for a wide range of musical styles and cultures.
courses.offering_note: Semester Course (Anticipated Fall 2027); Listed under 'Future Offerings': potential future offering; offerings shift based on enrollment and need

courses.department: Fine Arts: Visual Arts, Music, Theater
courses.description: This music course is a comprehensive class in understanding electronic music and sound production design and techniques. In this semester-long course, students explore the intricacies of sound and music for film, electronic composition, and audio methods. This course is designed to provide students with instruction in the use of a computer for composing original music. Topics will include, but are not limited to music theory, history of electronic music, listening and analysis, form and structure, synthesizers, midi instruments and software, audio recording, mixing and effects, remix, sampling and copyright, live performance, film scoring and podcasting. Students will use MIDI and software to complete a variety of film and music production projects.
courses.offering_note: Semester Course (Anticipated Spring 2028); Listed under 'Future Offerings': potential future offering; offerings shift based on enrollment and need

courses.department: Fine Arts: Visual Arts, Music, Theater
courses.description: This course is for students with an interest in dance. We will begin each class with a warm-up on stage. Over the semester students will learn routines in various techniques such as tap, ballet, hip hop, jazz, and modern dance. Dance students will examine, question, celebrate, and reflect on a multitude of dance traditions and functions from around the world. Students will perform dances at both our Fall and Spring Night of The Arts events. Students will learn techniques to choreograph a dance together as the final project in this course. No prior dance experience is necessary. Please note this class meets after school. This course is open to students in grades 7-12.
courses.notes: Theater; open to students in grades 7-12; meets after school

courses.department: Fine Arts: Visual Arts, Music, Theater
courses.description: Class will be held on stage in the auditorium. This course is highly collaborative and will exercise your creative muscles to exhaustion! There are two components to this course, performance and production. Students will hone their acting skills as well as learn basic techniques in sewing, prop construction, makeup, and set design for the theatre. This class will attend at least one live performance during the school year. Students who are actively involved in RU’s Drama program are encouraged to enroll. This course is open to students in grades 9-12.

Learn the skills necessary to develop lifelong fitness. Team sports and individual fitness activities are used as a vehicle for introducing strategies for assessing personal fitness levels, goal-setting, and building a foundation for understanding the health and skill-related components of physical fitness. My Physical Best I provides an experience through which all students recognize the value of physical activity for health, enjoyment, challenge, self- expression and/or social interaction.

Deepen your understanding of the health and skill-related components of physical fitness through an array of team sports and individual-performance activities. It is strongly recommended that all students complete My Physical Best I (MPB1) prior to this course. A basic understanding of the principles of training, target heart rates, and the FITT formula as they apply to personal fitness levels will be essential for your success. The concept of wellness and the importance of striving for optimal levels of health are the cornerstones of this course and are exemplified by a capstone project where students develop and maintain a personal fitness portfolio.

RU Health Education is designed to assist students in developing life skills to maintain and improve their health, prevent disease, and reduce health-related risk behaviors. The course allows students to acquire and demonstrate health-related knowledge, skills, and practices. The course is required for one semester. Topics of instruction include: Adolescent Brain Development, Personality/Psychology, Behavior Modification/Change, Stress Management, Depression/Suicide Prevention, Loss/Grieving, Chemical Addiction, Media Literacy, Human Sexuality/Relationships. The “Reality Works” baby project is a requirement for completion of the course. Historically, students have taken this class in 10th grade, but this semester-long class is open to students in any high school grade.
courses.fulfills_text: The course is required for one semester.
courses.notes: Health; historically taken in 10th grade, open to any high school grade

courses.description: Life Skills is designed to increase student knowledge and skills necessary for everyday living that will serve them well in their postsecondary lives. The course emphasizes goal-setting, decision making and problem solving, communication, healthy lifestyles and relationships, nutrition, personal safety, citizenship and consumerism. The curriculum will offer students the emotional, social and intellectual tools needed to achieve success in life – on a personal level, an interpersonal level, and within their community and work places.
courses.notes: Health > Life Skills sub-heading; description begins 'Life Skills is designed...'

courses.description: The Driver Education program at RU is based on basic driving systems. The focus is to assist students in becoming low-risk motor vehicle operators. Emphasis is placed on responsibility in every aspect of their participation in this course. Students will have to demonstrate that they possess the maturity, responsibility, and skill potential for operator license possession. The Driver Education department at RU recognizes that thirty hours of classroom and six hours of behind the wheel instruction cannot produce a skilled driver without parental assistance and support. The number one killer of youth ages 15-20 is traffic crashes. Parents, students, and teachers, working together, can be much more successful at turning this statistic around. Prerequisites : A student must have his/her permit prior to the first day of class and a copy of the permit must be given to Student Services one month prior to the first day of the class. Students must sign up for Driver's Education by June 1st for the upcoming fall semester and by December 1st for the upcoming spring semester. There is limited space in Driver’s Education classes. Registration will only be permitted if there are open seats. Seniors will be given preference only if registering, and having their permit, prior to the deadlines noted above. Prior to the deadline, non-seniors will be registered based on the date of procurement of permit, not by date of sign up for the course. Any open seats after the registration deadlines will be available for those with a permit on a first come, first served basis.
